o: We build a loop from the given strings in order, optionally reversing each one, then cut it at some position to form a linear string; we want the lexicographically largest possible result. In Example 1, choosing "cba" and "xyz" and cutting inside "cba" right before 'z' yields "zyxcba". In Example 2 there is a single string, so we simply take its better orientation, "cba". Since total length is at most 1000, even an $O(L^2)$ scan over all cut points is fast, but a greedy observation lets us restrict which strings need to be examined as cut hosts.
k: Each string contributes either itself or its reversal to the loop; for any fixed cut location, the rest of the loop should use each string's lexicographically larger orientation.
The answer must start with the globally largest achievable character, so the cut can only lie inside a string whose best orientation starts with that maximum character.
With total length L ≤ 1000, trying every cut point of every candidate is at most O(L^2) character work — easily fast enough.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force over All Orientations and Cut Points
a.i: For every string, try both orientations (original and reversed), and for every cut point inside it, build the full linear string: suffix of the chosen orientation + prefix of it + all remaining strings in their better orientations. Take the maximum over all candidates. This directly simulates the problem definition and, since total length is small, runs comfortably within limits.
s: Precompute nothing initially; define a helper that returns max(s, reversed(s)) for a string.
For each index i and each orientation o of strs[i], for each cut index j in [0, len):
Build candidate = o[j:] + o[:j] + concat(best(strs[k]) for k != i).
a.t: O(L^2) where L is total length — for each of up to L cut points we build and compare an O(L)-length string.
a.sp: O(L) for the concatenated helper strings and candidates.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Restriction of Cut Hosts
a.i: Every character of the answer comes from some string's better orientation, so the whole loop minus the cut host should use max(s, reverse(s)). Moreover, the answer's first character is the largest character achievable anywhere, so the cut must fall inside a string whose best orientation begins with that global maximum character. We only enumerate cut points inside such strings, cutting their search space dramatically while producing identical results.
s: Compute b[i] = max(strs[i], reverse(strs[i])) for all i.
Find m = the largest first character among all b[i].
For each i whose b[i][0] == m, for each cut j in b[i], build candidate b[i][j:] + b[i][:j] + concatenation of all other b[k].
a.t: O(L^2) worst case still, but typically far fewer cut hosts are examined since only strings starting with the maximum character are considered; building each candidate costs O(L).
a.sp: O(L) for the precomputed orientations, rest-string, and candidates.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 to establish correctness quickly, then mention the greedy pruning of Approach 2 as an optimization. Common pitfalls: forgetting to also try the reversed orientation of the cut-host string, mishandling the single-string case (rest is empty), and off-by-one errors when splitting the loop (cut before vs after a character — iterating j over all positions covers both). Edge cases: one string, all identical characters, or a string that is a palindrome (orientation choice doesn't matter). Follow-ups might ask for an O(L) suffix-array/rotation-based solution or handling very large inputs where string comparison cost matters.
